title: Smart lighting technology enables remote color control
byline: National Research Council of Science and Technology
excerpt: Lighting has evolved from simply illuminating objects to changing their perceived colors. content_html:
Lighting has evolved from simply illuminating objects to changing their perceived colors. A smart lighting technology has been developed that changes how objects appear in color by adjusting only the light shining on them, without repainting the objects or modifying their surfaces. The technology can change the perceived color of specific objects while maintaining natural white illumination in the surrounding space. Visitors will be able to see how the same object appears in different colors at an exhibition to be held at the National Science Museum in Daejeon, South Korea, in November.

Dr. Suwan Jeon, senior researcher at the Department of Nano Display Research of the Nano Convergence Research Division at the Korea Institute of Machinery and Materials, has developed a smart lighting technology for remote color control that changes the perceived color of objects by precisely adjusting light at multiple wavelengths. Jeon established the principles of color control, developed an LED lighting system based on these principles and experimentally verified the resulting color changes.

The color of an object as perceived by the human eye depends on the light illuminating it. Even the same object can appear to have a different color when the incident light changes, as the light reflected from the object and reaching the eye also changes. Based on this principle, the technology makes objects appear in desired colors simply by adjusting the combination of light emitted from the lighting system, without attaching additional devices to the objects or modifying their surfaces.

Conventional lighting systems often change the overall color appearance of a space when the color of the illumination is adjusted. Jeon addressed this limitation by precisely controlling the brightness of multiple LEDs. This approach maintains natural white illumination in the surrounding space while changing the light reflected from a specific object, making only that object's perceived color appear different.

To evaluate the technology's performance, Jeon developed a lighting system using several types of LEDs along with a measurement system. Color-changing experiments were conducted using color cards and Morpho butterflies, which exhibit vivid structural colors. The experiments confirmed that the same object could appear in different colors depending on the combination of illuminating light. In the final system validation, the researchers observed color changes with a CIEDE2000 color difference (ΔE₀₀) value exceeding 90.

The developed technology could be applied to exhibitions, interior design, product design and artworks by creating various color effects simply through lighting changes, without altering the products or exhibits themselves. Its key advantage is the ability to change the perceived colors of objects to suit different spaces and purposes without repainting or replacing them.

Jeon has also collaborated with artist Geunho Park, who works under the name "Chamsae," to create an artwork titled "Changing Colors with Light" using the newly developed technology. The artwork will be exhibited at "2026 Artience Daejeon," held at the Future Technology Hall of the National Science Museum from Nov. 17 to 28, 2026. Visitors will be able to directly observe how the same object appears in different colors depending on the illuminating light.

Jeon, senior researcher at the Department of Nano Display Research at KIMM, emphasized, "The most distinctive feature of this technology is that it can change the perceived color of an object simply by adjusting the light shining on it, without changing the object itself. We expect this technology to open up new possibilities for color expression using light in exhibitions, spatial design, product presentation and the arts."
